summaryBox.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
summaryBox.takeaway: Dynamic equilibrium: r_f = r_b. Macroscopic concentrations remain constant. Pure solids/liquids are excluded.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM KINETICS
                     
   Rate ▲                                     Concentration ▲
        │ \  Forward Rate ($r_f$)                           │ \  [Reactants]
        │  \_______                                         │  \_______
        │   ─────── Rate Equilibrium ($r_f = r_b$)          │   ─────── [Equilibrium]
        │  /                                                │  /
        │ /  Backward Rate ($r_b$)                          │ /  [Products]
      0 └──────┴──────────────────► Time                  0 └──────┴──────────────────► Time
            Equilibrium Established                             Equilibrium Established
conceptBreakdown.content:
A chemical system achieves Dynamic Equilibrium in a closed container when the rate of the forward reaction ($r_f$) equals the rate of the reverse reaction ($r_b$), causing macroscopic concentrations of reactants and products to remain constant over time.

• **The Law of Mass Action (Guldberg & Waage, 1864)**: At a given temperature, the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations or partial pressures) of the reacting species raised to powers equal to their respective stoichiometric coefficients.

For a general reversible gaseous reaction:
$$a\text{A}(g) + b\text{B}(g) \rightleftharpoons c\text{C}(g) + d\text{D}(g)$$
$$\mathbf{K_c = \frac{[\text{C}]^c [\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a [\text{B}]^b}} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{K_p = \frac{P_C^c P_D^d}{P_A^a P_B^b}}$$

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.2 Mathematical Inter-Relationships Between K_p, K_c, and K_x
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.2 Mathematical Inter-Relationships Between K_p, K_c, and K_x
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
UNITS & Δn_g DEPENDENCE
                       
   If Δn_g = 0 ⟹ K_p = K_c = K_x (Dimensionless, e.g., H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI)
   If Δn_g > 0 ⟹ K_p > K_c (Units: bar^Δn_g or M^Δn_g, e.g., PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂)
   If Δn_g < 0 ⟹ K_p < K_c (e.g., N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃)
conceptBreakdown.content:
Applying the Ideal Gas Law ($P_i = \frac{n_i}{V} RT = [C_i] RT$):
$$\mathbf{K_p = K_c (RT)^{\Delta n_g}}$$
where $\Delta n_g = (c + d) - (a + b)$ is the net change in gaseous moles.

• **Relation with Mole Fraction Constant ($K_x$)**:
$$\mathbf{K_p = K_x (P_{\text{total}})^{\Delta n_g}} \quad \vert \quad \mathbf{K_c = K_x \left( \frac{P_{\text{total}}}{RT} \right)^{\Delta n_g}}$$

• **Heterogeneous Equilibrium Rule**: Pure solids and pure liquids have constant active masses ($\text{activity} = 1.0$) and are EXCLUDED from equilibrium constant expressions (e.g., for $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$, $K_c = [\text{CO}_2]$ and $K_p = P_{\text{CO}_2}$).

quickRevision: When Δn_g = 0, K_p = K_c = K_x and the constant is dimensionless.
Pure solids and liquids have activity = 1.0 and are excluded from K expressions.
